prompt: What makes a method a higher-order function?
hint: Look at its parameters and its return type.

choices.text: It is generic, declared with `<T>`
choices.why: `select` is generic, but that is a separate property.

choices.text: It takes or returns a function
choices.why: Right: a functional interface as a parameter or return type.

choices.text: It calls itself on a smaller input until it reaches a base case
choices.why: That is recursion.

choices.text: It runs on more than one thread
choices.why: Nothing about threads is involved.

prompt: In `select(items, rule)`, which part belongs to `select` and which to the caller?
hint: The part that is always the same.

choices.text: `select` decides which items pass; the caller builds the list
choices.why: The other way round: the rule decides, `select` builds the list.

choices.text: `select` owns the loop and the new list; the caller supplies the test
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Both are written by the caller each time
choices.why: Then there would be nothing to reuse.

choices.text: `select` owns everything; the lambda is only a label
choices.why: The lambda is the test that runs for every item.

prompt: A rule passed to `select` prints a line each time it is called. How many lines will it print?
hint: Who decides when the lambda runs?

choices.text: One, when the lambda is written
choices.why: Writing it runs nothing.

choices.text: One per item that passes the test
choices.why: It prints before it knows its answer, so every call prints.

choices.text: As many as `select` calls it: once per item here
choices.why: Right. The effect happens as often as the method decides to call.

choices.text: None: `select` suppresses output from rules
choices.why: It calls the rule as written.

choices.text: The books with 450 pages or more
choices.why: It has no books to look at; it returns a test.

choices.text: A `Predicate<Book>` that remembers 450
choices.why: Right: a test with the number captured.

choices.text: `true`, because 450 is at least 0
choices.why: It returns a lambda, not a `boolean`.

choices.text: The number of pages, 450, boxed as an `Integer`
choices.why: The number is captured inside, not returned.

hint: 8990 minus 15% of it, rounded down to the cent.

prompt: `lumen` and `atlas` both come from `orderNumbers`. Why did asking `atlas` not move `lumen` on?

choices.text: Each call to `orderNumbers` made its own counter
choices.why: Right, and each closure captured a different one.

choices.text: `AtomicInteger` gives each thread a separate value
choices.why: One thread ran this; the counters are separate objects.

choices.text: The prefixes are different strings, and the counter is keyed by them
choices.why: There is no map of counters, only one per closure.

choices.text: `Supplier` resets its state after each `get`
choices.why: `lumen` went 1, 2, then 3.

prompt: Why may the lambda in `orderNumbers` capture `next` and change the counter, when lesson 1 refused `count++`?
hint: The rule is about the variable.

choices.text: Atomics are exempt from the effectively final rule
choices.why: No type is exempt.

choices.text: `incrementAndGet` runs outside the lambda
choices.why: It runs inside, on each `get`.

choices.text: `next` always points at the same object; only that object changes
choices.why: Right. `count++` reassigns the variable itself.

choices.text: Lambdas returned from a method follow looser rules
choices.why: The same rule applies everywhere.

prompt: A function together with the values it captured is called a ___.
`Wrappers.java` asked for five titles. How many times did `authorOf` really run?
`memoized(logged(f))` logged only the misses. What would `logged(memoized(f))` log?
hint: The outermost wrapper sees every call.

choices.text: The same three lines
choices.why: The logger is now outside the cache, so it sees the hits too.

choices.text: Every call, hits included
choices.why: Right: five lines.

choices.text: Nothing, because the cache swallows the log
choices.why: The cache is inside; the logger runs first.

choices.text: Only the first call, after which the cache is full
choices.why: Each new title is a miss; the logger sees all calls anyway.

prompt: Which of these functions are safe to wrap in `memoized`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Same argument, same answer, and nothing else that matters.

choices.text: The square of a number
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: The current price of a book, read from a database
choices.why: No: the price changes, and the cache would keep the old one.

choices.text: The author of a title, from a fixed table
choices.why: Yes, like `authorOf`.

choices.text: Today's date formatted for a title page
choices.why: No: tomorrow it would still say today.

prompt: Why does `Strategies.java` refuse an unknown rule name instead of using `getOrDefault(name, cents -> cents)`?

choices.text: `getOrDefault` does not accept a lambda as its default
choices.why: It accepts any value of the map's type.

choices.text: A typo would silently charge full price
choices.why: Right. A plausible wrong number is worse than an error.

choices.text: A `TreeMap` throws on a missing key, so the program has no choice
choices.why: `get` returns `null` on a missing key.

choices.text: The default would be slower than an error
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

prompt: With rules in a map, what does adding a new pricing rule take?

choices.text: A new class and a new branch in a `switch`
choices.why: That is the classic pattern the map replaces.

choices.text: One more entry in the map
choices.why: Right: a name and a lambda.

choices.text: A new functional interface for that rule
choices.why: All rules share `UnaryOperator<Long>`.

choices.text: Recompiling the JDK's `java.util.function`
choices.why: Nothing in the JDK changes.

prompt: Each strategy now needs a label for logs, a configuration value and two related methods. What does the lesson suggest?

choices.text: Keep the map and put the extras in comments

choices.text: One lambda per strategy that returns an `Object[]` with the extras
